lessons.title: Common Mistakes When Moving From Residential to Commercial

children.text: Most Indians who buy commercial property have already owned a flat or two. That experience feels like an advantage. It is often the opposite. Habits that work perfectly well with homes, such as comparing price per sq ft with the building next door, signing a template agreement, trusting a broker's yield figure or reinvesting sale proceeds in "property", can quietly destroy value in commercial real estate. This final lesson collects the mistakes that repeatedly catch investors making the move, shows what each one costs, and gives you the habit to replace it with.

body.text: When you move from residential to commercial property, you stop buying a home and start buying a business: a lease, a tenant and a stream of cash. Evaluate it the way you would evaluate a business, not a flat.

children.text: The Mistakes at a Glance

body.caption: Ten common mistakes and what to do instead

cells: 1. Trusting the gross yield
"9% yield" quoted before costs and vacancy
Calculate net yield after owner costs and a vacancy allowance
2. Pricing by sq ft
"Cheaper per sq ft than the unit next door"
Value on net income divided by a realistic cap rate
3. Buying vacant or under-construction units on hope
"Tenants will line up once it is ready"
Prefer leased units with verified tenants, or price in a long vacancy
4. Ignoring the lock-in
Strong tenant, but lock-in ends in months
Check remaining lock-in and negotiate an extension before buying
5. Not verifying the rent
A lease that exists only on paper, or a tenant related to the seller
Verify through bank statements, Form 26AS or AIS, GST records and company checks
6. Accepting "assured returns"
Developer promises 10% to 12% for a few years
Ask what the price would be without the guarantee and what happens after it ends
7. Ignoring the building
Focusing on the unit, not its owners, upkeep and age
Check ownership structure, vacancy in the building and upgrade plans
8. Using residential paperwork habits
Template lease, vague clauses, handshake terms
Have a lawyer draft or review lock-in, escalation, CAM, force majeure and exit clauses
9. Assuming residential tax rules apply
Expecting to reinvest sale proceeds tax-free in any property
Plan capital gains, GST and TDS with a CA before buying or selling
10. Over-leveraging and over-concentrating
Large LRD on one unit, no cash reserve
Match loan tenure to lock-in, keep a vacancy reserve, diversify with REITs

children.text: Mistake 1: Trusting the Gross Yield

A broker shows you a shop in a Noida market: price ₹1 crore, rent ₹75,000 a month, "9% yield". The lease, however, makes the owner pay CAM of ₹12,000 a month. Property tax is ₹50,000 a year. And any sensible investor should allow for vacancy and re-leasing costs, say 10% of rent a year over the long run.

body.title: From headline to reality: yield on a ₹1 crore shop (%)

children.text: The "9% yield" is really about 6.2% before income tax. Still better than most flats, but a completely different investment decision from the one the broker presented. Always ask for the lease and rebuild the net number yourself.
Mistakes 2 and 3: Pricing by Sq Ft and Buying on Hope

Residential buyers are trained to ask "what is the rate per sq ft?". In commercial property, a vacant unit at ₹9,000 per sq ft is not a bargain compared with a leased unit at ₹12,000 next door. The leased unit comes with income. The vacant one comes with months of zero rent, a rent-free period, brokerage and uncertainty about what tenant, if any, will sign. Price commercial units on income and cap rate, and for vacant units, subtract the realistic cost of getting them leased.

body.text: Under-construction commercial projects sold with "assured returns" or "lease guarantees" combine several mistakes at once: no tenant, construction risk, often strata ownership, and a guarantee that is usually priced into an inflated purchase price. When the guarantee period ends, the rent depends on a market that may pay far less. Chapter 3 worked through one such pitch in detail.

children.text: Mistakes 4 and 5: The Lease Is Weaker Than It Looks

Two lease problems catch experienced flat owners off guard. The first is buying a unit with a strong tenant whose lock-in ends soon, which leaves you paying a secure-income price for insecure income. The second is more dangerous: a lease that makes rent look higher than the market would pay, often because the tenant is connected to the seller.

markDefs.definition: A lease where the tenant is connected to the seller or developer, for example a company owned by the seller's family. Such leases can be set at above-market rents to inflate the sale price, then renegotiated or ended after the sale.

children.text: In a
related-party lease

, a seller leases the unit to a company they control at an inflated rent, sells to an investor at a price based on that rent, and then the tenant leaves or renegotiates soon after. The overpayment can be enormous.

body.caption: Monthly rents; ignores owner costs for simplicity.

children.text: Example: a 1,200 sq ft office in Gurugram leased at ₹1.2 lakh a month when similar units rent for ₹90,000. At an 8% cap rate, the inflated rent supports a price of ₹14.4 lakh ÷ 0.08 = ₹1.8 crore, while market rent supports only ₹10.8 lakh ÷ 0.08 = ₹1.35 crore. An investor who pays ₹1.8 crore has overpaid by ₹45 lakh the day the lease is renegotiated.

body.title: Red flags that a lease may not be what it seems

children.text: Rent well above comparable units in the same building. A tenant company that is recently incorporated, very small, or shares directors or an address with the seller or developer. A lease signed shortly before the sale. Rent paid in cash, irregularly, or not reflected in TDS records. A very short lock-in despite a supposedly committed tenant. Reluctance by the seller to let you speak to the tenant.

Checks: search the tenant company and its directors on the MCA portal, verify rent credits in bank statements, match TDS entries in the seller's Form 26AS or AIS, and compare passing rent with at least three recent leases nearby.

body.label: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) portal
body.description: Look up a tenant company's incorporation date, directors and filing status. Shared directors or addresses with the seller are a warning sign of a related-party lease.

children.text: Mistakes 7 and 8: Forgetting the Building and the Paperwork

columns.label: Residential habit
points: Judge the flat, ignore the building's ownership
Renew every 11 months and adjust as you go
Let the broker handle the details

columns.label: Commercial practice
points: Judge the building: owners, upkeep, vacancy and age
Lawyer-drafted lease with clear lock-in, escalation, CAM and exit terms
Negotiate once for years; the lease sets your income
Income and exit cap rate decide the return, so mistakes compound

children.text: Mistakes 9 and 10: Tax Surprises and Too Much Risk in One Place

Owners who sell a flat to buy commercial property often assume the sale proceeds can roll over tax-free. They cannot. Reinvesting a residential gain tax-free requires buying another residential house, and there is no exemption for reinvesting in commercial property, leaving specified bonds of up to ₹50 lakh as the main alternative. New commercial landlords are also surprised by GST registration once rent crosses the threshold, TDS reconciliation and tenant paperwork.

Finally, many investors put their entire property budget into one commercial unit, sometimes with a large LRD loan whose tenure runs years beyond the tenant's lock-in. One tenant exit then threatens both the income and the loan. A cash reserve of about a year's rent, a lock-in that covers much of the loan tenure, and part of the allocation in diversified REITs turn a fragile position into a resilient one.

stats.label: Tax on an ₹80 lakh gain moved into commercial

body.text: Every mistake in this lesson has the same root: treating a lease as a detail when it is the asset. If you remember one thing from this course, make it this: in commercial property, read the lease before you look at the building, and look at the building before you look at the price.

body.title: Calculate: Fixing a Broker's Yield
body.prompt: A shop in Jayanagar, Bengaluru is priced at ₹1.2 crore with rent of ₹85,000 a month, advertised as an 8.5% yield. The owner pays CAM of ₹10,000 a month and property tax of ₹60,000 a year. Allow 10% of annual rent for vacancy and re-leasing. What is the net yield, in %? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Annual rent: ₹10.2 lakh. CAM: ₹1.2 lakh. Property tax: ₹0.6 lakh. Vacancy allowance: ₹1.02 lakh. Net: ₹10.2 lakh minus ₹2.82 lakh = ₹7.38 lakh. Net yield: ₹7.38 lakh ÷ ₹120 lakh × 100 = 6.15%.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Inflated Lease
body.textWithBlank: A lease where the tenant is connected to the seller, sometimes used to inflate rent before a sale, is called a ___ lease.
body.explanation: Related-party leases can make a property look far more valuable than market rent would justify. Check tenant ownership and compare rent with nearby leases.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Is the Real Bargain?
body.question: In the same Pune building, Unit X is vacant at ₹9,000 per sq ft. Unit Y is leased to a listed company with 5 years of lock-in left at ₹12,000 per sq ft and an 8% net yield. Which statement reflects commercial thinking?
options: Unit X is the bargain because it is 25% cheaper per sq ft
Unit Y should be judged on its income and lease security, while Unit X's price must allow for vacancy, rent-free months and leasing risk
Both are worth the same because they are in the same building
Unit X is better because you can choose your own tenant
body.explanation: Commercial value comes from income. Unit Y delivers secure rent now. Unit X has no income, and its real cost includes months of vacancy, a rent-free period, brokerage and uncertainty, so a lower sq ft price is not automatically cheaper.

body.title: Scenario: Rakesh's Big Move
body.scenario: Rakesh, 50, is selling his two rented flats in Noida for ₹1.8 crore after costs, with a long-term capital gain of ₹80 lakh. Tired of 2% to 3% rental yields, he plans to put all of it into a shop in an under-construction mall in Greater Noida West. The developer offers a "10% assured return for 3 years" and a 20% discount on the per sq ft rate compared with a finished mall nearby. He expects to reinvest without paying capital gains tax because "it is all property".
body.prompt: Identify the mistakes in Rakesh's plan and suggest what he should do instead.
body.modelAnswer: At least six mistakes. First, tax: moving a residential gain into commercial property gets no rollover exemption, so 12.5% of ₹80 lakh, about ₹10 lakh plus surcharge and cess, is due unless he buys a residential house or uses specified bonds of up to ₹50 lakh. Second, the assured return is almost certainly priced into the purchase price and ends after 3 years. Third, the unit is under construction and has no tenant, adding delay and leasing risk. Fourth, a shop in a mall sold unit by unit risks the strata-mall problem, with no single owner managing the tenant mix. Fifth, the 20% sq ft discount is meaningless without income; it may reflect exactly those risks. Sixth, putting all ₹1.8 crore into one unit is extreme concentration, with a very narrow exit. Instead, he could consider a completed, pre-leased unit with a verified strong tenant and a long lock-in, bought after checking the building and lease, alongside listed REITs for diversified commercial income. He should also plan the capital gains tax, including whether bonds or a residential purchase make sense, with a CA before selling the flats.

body.title: Final Checklist Before Your First Commercial Purchase
steps: Rebuild the net yield yourself from the lease: owner costs, vacancy allowance, then tax
Value the property on net income and a realistic cap rate, not price per sq ft
Confirm the tenant is real, unrelated to the seller and financially sound
Compare passing rent with at least three recent comparable leases
Check remaining lock-in, escalation dates and exit rights
Assess the building: ownership structure, age, vacancy, upkeep and approvals
Have a lawyer review the lease and title
Plan capital gains, GST and TDS with a CA
Match any loan to the lock-in and keep about a year's rent in reserve
Decide how much to hold directly and how much through diversified REITs

points: Residential habits such as trusting sq ft rates, template agreements and broker yields are the main source of commercial property mistakes.
Always rebuild the net yield; a "9% yield" can shrink to around 6% after owner costs and a vacancy allowance.
Price commercial property on income and cap rate; vacant units must be discounted for the cost and risk of leasing them.
Verify every lease: short lock-ins and related-party tenants can hide large overpayments.
Selling flats to buy commercial property has no tax-free rollover; plan capital gains before you sell.
Protect yourself with a cash reserve, sensible leverage and diversification, and read the lease before the building and the building before the price.

children.text: That completes the course. You can now tell the difference between a home and a business wearing the same "real estate" label, price each on its true economics, and choose the route, direct residential, direct commercial or REITs, that fits your capital, goals and temperament.

body.text: Examples, prices, rents and tax figures in this lesson are illustrative and simplified. Tax and regulatory rules change; confirm current law with qualified professionals. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any property or investment.
